contaminantRules.detail: Conventional wheat, oats, barley, and rye are routinely sprayed with glyphosate (Roundup) as a pre-harvest drying agent. USDA and independent testing detects glyphosate residue in the majority of conventional grain products.
contaminantRules.title: Glyphosate residue likely

contaminantRules.detail: Conventional US corn is the single largest use of atrazine (an EU-banned endocrine disruptor) and glyphosate. Residues are routinely detected in corn-derived ingredients.
contaminantRules.title: Atrazine & glyphosate residue likely

contaminantRules.detail: Over 90% of US soybeans are genetically modified for glyphosate tolerance (Roundup Ready) and increasingly 2,4-D. Residues are common in conventional soy-derived ingredients.
contaminantRules.title: Glyphosate & 2,4-D residue likely

contaminantRules.detail: Conventional canola is genetically modified for glyphosate tolerance and is also typically chemically extracted with hexane.
contaminantRules.title: Glyphosate residue likely

contaminantRules.detail: Roughly half of US sugar comes from genetically modified sugar beets sprayed with glyphosate.
contaminantRules.title: Glyphosate residue possible (sugar beet)

contaminantRules.detail: Conventional cotton is GMO for glyphosate and dicamba tolerance, and is regulated as a non-food crop — meaning pesticide tolerances are higher than for food crops.
contaminantRules.title: Glyphosate & dicamba residue likely

contaminantRules.detail: Microwave popcorn bags are commonly lined with PFAS forever chemicals to resist grease. PFAS migrates into the food during heating.
contaminantRules.title: PFAS exposure likely (packaging)

contaminantRules.detail: Non-stick and fluoropolymer surfaces are part of the PFAS family. They shed microparticles into food and release toxic fumes when overheated.
contaminantRules.title: PFAS / PTFE exposure

contaminantRules.detail: Grease-resistant wrappers, pizza boxes, bakery liners, and microwave-ready coated papers frequently contain PFAS coatings that migrate into food during storage and heating.
contaminantRules.title: PFAS-coated packaging possible

contaminantRules.detail: Fast-food wrappers, sandwich and burger papers, fry boxes, and clamshell containers are frequently treated with PFAS forever chemicals for grease resistance. FDA testing has repeatedly detected PFAS migration into food from these materials.
contaminantRules.title: PFAS exposure likely (fast-food packaging)

contaminantRules.detail: Molded-fiber "compostable" bowls and takeout containers were long treated with PFAS for grease and moisture resistance. Independent testing has found high fluorine levels in many of these products.
contaminantRules.title: PFAS exposure possible (compostable fiber packaging)

contaminantRules.detail: PFAS forever chemicals bioaccumulate in fish and shellfish from contaminated water. Freshwater fish in particular carry some of the highest PFAS levels measured in any food; the EPA and FDA monitor PFAS in seafood. PFOS, a common PFAS in fish, is an IARC Group 2B possible human carcinogen.
contaminantRules.title: PFAS accumulation possible (seafood)

contaminantRules.detail: PFAS are widespread drinking-water contaminants. Independent testing has detected PFAS in a number of bottled and spring waters, and the EPA has set enforceable limits for PFAS in drinking water.
contaminantRules.title: PFAS possible (bottled water)

contaminantRules.detail: Leafy greens take up PFAS from soil and irrigation water — especially near contaminated sites or where sewage-sludge "biosolids" were applied as fertilizer. Leafy vegetables show higher PFAS uptake than most other produce.
contaminantRules.title: PFAS uptake possible (leafy greens)

contaminantRules.detail: Rice takes up inorganic arsenic — an IARC Group 1 known human carcinogen — from soil and water far more than other grains. The FDA specifically tracks arsenic in rice and infant rice cereal under its "Closer to Zero" program.
contaminantRules.title: Inorganic arsenic likely (rice)

contaminantRules.detail: Independent testing (Consumer Reports, As You Sow) repeatedly finds lead and cadmium in cocoa and dark chocolate. Cadmium is an IARC Group 1 known human carcinogen; lead is a cumulative neurotoxin with no safe level for children.
contaminantRules.title: Lead & cadmium likely (cocoa)

contaminantRules.detail: Large predatory fish accumulate methylmercury, a potent neurotoxin the FDA and EPA advise children and pregnant women to limit. Methylmercury is classified by IARC as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans).
contaminantRules.title: Methylmercury likely (predatory fish)

contaminantRules.detail: The FDA has issued repeated recalls for lead-contaminated cinnamon and other ground spices, some intentionally adulterated to boost weight and color. Lead is a cumulative neurotoxin with no safe level for children.
contaminantRules.title: Lead contamination possible (spices)

contaminantRules.detail: The FDA sets action levels for inorganic arsenic and lead in apple and grape juice after repeated detections. Inorganic arsenic is an IARC Group 1 known human carcinogen.
contaminantRules.title: Arsenic & lead possible (fruit juice)

contaminantRules.detail: Clean Label Project and Consumer Reports testing has found lead, cadmium, and arsenic in many protein powders — especially plant-based ones, which concentrate metals from their crops.
contaminantRules.title: Heavy metals possible (protein powder)

contaminantRules.detail: Acrylamide forms when starchy foods are fried, baked, or roasted at high temperatures. It is classified by IARC as a Group 2A probable human carcinogen, and the FDA publishes guidance for reducing it.
contaminantRules.title: Acrylamide likely (high-heat starch)

ingredients.alternative: Organic cane sugar, maple syrup, raw honey, or dates.
ingredients.concern: Linked to obesity, fatty liver disease, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome.
ingredients.purpose: Cheap sweetener that extends shelf life and adds bulk.

ingredients.alternative: Cold-pressed olive oil, avocado oil, or grass-fed butter.
ingredients.concern: Trans fats — directly linked to heart disease. Banned by the FDA in 2018 but still appears in some products.
ingredients.purpose: Improves texture and extends shelf life.

ingredients.alternative: Vitamin E (tocopherols) or rosemary extract.
ingredients.concern: Listed by the National Toxicology Program as 'reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen.'
ingredients.purpose: Synthetic preservative that prevents fats from going rancid.

ingredients.alternative: Vitamin E or rosemary extract.
ingredients.concern: Possible endocrine disruptor and tumor promoter in animal studies.

ingredients.alternative: Natural antioxidants like vitamin E.
ingredients.concern: Linked to immune system dysfunction and behavioral effects in studies.
ingredients.purpose: Synthetic preservative used in processed foods and frying oils.

ingredients.alternative: Uncured meats preserved with celery powder and sea salt.
ingredients.concern: Forms nitrosamines when heated — Group 1 IARC carcinogen when used in processed meats.
ingredients.purpose: Preserves color and prevents botulism in cured meats.

ingredients.alternative: Beet juice, paprika extract, or annatto.
ingredients.concern: Linked to hyperactivity in children. Banned or warning-labeled in much of Europe.

ingredients.alternative: Turmeric or annatto.
ingredients.concern: Allergen and hyperactivity trigger. Requires warning labels in the EU.

ingredients.alternative: Turmeric, saffron, or annatto.
ingredients.concern: May contain carcinogenic contaminants. Hyperactivity link in children.

ingredients.alternative: Spirulina extract or red cabbage.
ingredients.concern: Petroleum-based dye, hyperactivity concerns in children.

ingredients.alternative: Avoid products that need to look unnaturally white.
ingredients.concern: Banned in the EU in 2022 over DNA damage concerns. Still allowed in US foods.
ingredients.purpose: Whitens and brightens candies, dairy, and powdered foods.

ingredients.alternative: Glass, stainless steel, or uncoated paper packaging.
ingredients.concern: Forever chemical that bioaccumulates and never breaks down. IARC reclassified PFOA as a Group 1 known human carcinogen in 2024. Linked to kidney and testicular cancer, thyroid disease, and immune suppression.
ingredients.purpose: Historically used to make non-stick coatings, grease-resistant food wrappers, and stain-proof packaging.

ingredients.alternative: PFAS-free packaging and cookware.
ingredients.concern: Forever chemical classified by IARC as a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B). Persists in the body and the environment for decades.
ingredients.purpose: Used in stain repellents, food packaging coatings, and firefighting foam.

ingredients.alternative: Unwrapped or paper-wrapped foods from sources that explicitly state PFAS-free packaging.
ingredients.concern: Umbrella term for thousands of synthetic 'forever chemicals' that do not break down in the body or environment. Linked to cancer, immune dysfunction, hormone disruption, and developmental harm.
ingredients.purpose: Grease- and water-resistant coatings on fast-food wrappers, microwave popcorn bags, takeout containers, and pizza boxes.

ingredients.alternative: Cast iron, stainless steel, carbon steel, or ceramic-coated cookware.
ingredients.concern: Synthetic fluoropolymer in the PFAS family. Can shed microparticles into food and releases toxic fumes when overheated. Manufactured using other PFAS.
ingredients.purpose: Non-stick cookware coatings and processing equipment surfaces.

ingredients.alternative: Avoid products with fluorinated or 'non-stick' food contact materials.
ingredients.concern: Replacement chemical for PFOA that has been shown in EPA studies to cause similar liver, kidney, and immune-system damage. Still a forever chemical.
ingredients.purpose: Newer generation PFAS used in food contact materials.

ingredients.alternative: Certified organic or 'Glyphosate Residue Free' verified products.
ingredients.concern: World's most widely used herbicide. Classified by IARC as a Group 2A probable human carcinogen. Routinely detected as a residue on conventional wheat, oats, soy, and corn products. Endocrine disruptor and gut-microbiome disruptor.
ingredients.purpose: Broad-spectrum weed killer and pre-harvest desiccant on grains.

ingredients.alternative: Certified organic corn and grain products.
ingredients.concern: Endocrine disruptor banned in the European Union since 2004. Linked to birth defects, hormone disruption, and reproductive harm. Heavily applied to US corn — frequent groundwater contaminant.
ingredients.purpose: Herbicide used on conventional corn, sorghum, and sugarcane.

ingredients.alternative: Certified organic grain and meat products.
ingredients.concern: IARC Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans). A component of Agent Orange. Linked to non-Hodgkin lymphoma in agricultural worker studies.
ingredients.purpose: Broadleaf herbicide used on conventional grains, lawns, and pastures.

ingredients.alternative: Certified organic or non-GMO verified products.
ingredients.concern: Volatile herbicide notorious for drift damage to neighboring farms. Suspected endocrine and developmental toxicant.
ingredients.purpose: Broadleaf herbicide paired with genetically modified soy and cotton.

ingredients.alternative: Certified organic produce, especially for children's foods.
ingredients.concern: Organophosphate insecticide linked to lower IQ, ADHD, and developmental delays in children. Banned for food use in the US in 2021, but residues persist on imported produce.
ingredients.purpose: Insecticide on conventional fruits, vegetables, and nuts.

ingredients.alternative: Certified organic products.
ingredients.concern: One of the most acutely toxic herbicides in use. Strong epidemiological link to Parkinson's disease. Banned in the EU and over 30 other countries; still used in the US.
ingredients.purpose: Herbicide on conventional soy, corn, cotton, and orchard crops.

ingredients.alternative: Certified organic produce and grains.
ingredients.concern: IARC Group 2A probable human carcinogen. Organophosphate that interferes with the nervous system.
ingredients.purpose: Insecticide on conventional grain, fruit, and vegetable crops.

ingredients.alternative: Certified organic produce.
ingredients.concern: Systemic insecticides absorbed into the entire plant — cannot be washed off. Drivers of pollinator collapse. Detected in conventional baby foods and produce.
ingredients.purpose: Seed treatments and sprays on conventional fruits, vegetables, and grains.

ingredients.alternative: Lower-fat or plant-based protein sources from clean watersheds.
ingredients.concern: IARC Group 2A probable human carcinogen. Banned for US agricultural use in 1972 but still detected in fatty fish, dairy, and meat due to bioaccumulation in soil and water.

ingredients.alternative: Stevia, monk fruit, or raw honey in moderation.
ingredients.concern: Classified as 'possibly carcinogenic to humans' by the WHO in 2023.

ingredients.alternative: Stevia or monk fruit.
ingredients.concern: May disrupt gut microbiome and produce harmful compounds when heated.

ingredients.alternative: Stevia or monk fruit.
ingredients.concern: Animal studies suggest possible carcinogenicity; long-term human data is limited.
ingredients.purpose: Artificial sweetener, often blended with others.

ingredients.alternative: Mushrooms, tomatoes, parmesan, or sea salt for umami.
ingredients.concern: Triggers headaches and other symptoms in sensitive individuals.

ingredients.alternative: Agar, guar gum, or no thickener at all.

ingredients.purpose: Thickener and stabilizer derived from seaweed.

ingredients.alternative: Glycerin from natural sources.
ingredients.concern: Industrial solvent also used in antifreeze. Generally safe but a known irritant.

ingredients.alternative: Citric acid or refrigeration.
